title: Optimize walkthrough: prefetch & batching economics with Argus Insurance
summary: Redwood team demoed the Optimize console and a targeted cost model for Argus's claims assistant. Focus on prefix/KV cache patterns, batching tradeoffs, and hosted vs dedicated routing. Customer prioritized latency SLOs for UI flows and regulatory auditability for PII retention. Action items: run a 72-hour sandbox with sample traffic, share security whitepaper, and provide a tailored cost model spreadsheet.
action_items: Ben Cho: provision 72-hour sandbox with argus sample traces (due: 2028-02-15)
Alice Moreno: share tailored cost-model spreadsheet + pricing deck (due: 2028-02-10)
Priya Khatri: attach SOC2 summary and deployment checklist (due: 2028-02-11)
Raj Patel / Argus: provide 24h sample trace + latency SLOs (due: 2028-02-12)
next_steps: Start 72-hour sandbox with 50% production traffic cap
Schedule in-depth security review with Tom and Redwood security (week of 2028-02-13)
Redwood to deliver cost simulation of 3 scenarios: hosted baseline, dedicated fixed capacity, hybrid routing
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2028-02-08
Start: 15:30 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Alice (Redwood AE), Ben (Redwood SE), Priya (Redwood Solutions), Claire (Argus Eng Mgr), Raj (Argus SRE), Maya (Argus PM), Tom (Argus Security)

[00:00] Alice: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intro round — I'm Alice Moreno, AE on this account, Ben is going to lead the Optimize demo, and Priya will cover security and next steps. Claire, do you want to intro Argus folks?
[00:12] Claire: Yeah hi all, Claire here, lead on the claims assistant project. Raj is our infra lead, Maya is product, and Tom who will jump in on security questions. We're mainly looking at cost and latency for the UI flows, and audit / retention concerns for PII.
[00:26] Ben: Great, thanks. I'll jump into the Optimize console and run through three scenarios: naive hosted baseline, prefix/KV cache with continuous batching, and then a dedicated pool with routing policies. I'll also show the cost model per million tokens and some tradeoffs. A fair warning — some of the console names in the screen share might be slighly different if you look at earlier docs; we recently renamed a couple of knobs.
[01:02] Ben: (screen share) Okay, here's the Optimize dashboard. First slide — request distribution. I uploaded the sample trace you sent last week — nice work, Claire — this shows a heavy tail of short UI queries and a small percentage of long generation calls for policy explanations. That pattern screams prefix caching to me.
[01:35] Maya: Quick clarification: when you say prefix cache do you mean caching the tokenizer prefix or the KV cache for the model?
[01:40] Ben: Good question. We're talking about KV cache at the model level — basically store the key/value activations for the common prompts so subsequent requests with the same prefix skip the early layers. It reduces per-token compute. We also recommend a short-term prefix lookup layer to route hits to warm workers. Sometimes I say prefix cache and sometimes K-V cache, apologies, that's the same group of things here.
[02:05] Raj: How does that work with session affinity? our current infra is behind a load balancer that doesn't sticky sessions.
[02:12] Ben: Two options: session affinity at LB level to keep KV local, or a distributed KV store with low-latency lookup. For Argus's SLA I'd suggest sticky routing per user session for the short UI flows — that gives the best latency and cache hit. If you can't change LB, we can do routing based on user-id in the request header.
[02:44] Claire: Ok, what kind of hit rates are realistic? you showed a small tail earlier.
[02:50] Ben: With the mix you gave, a 40-60% effective KV hit is realistic after warm-up for top-n prompts. Our cost model assumes 50% average hit in scenario B. In practice you'll see variance; the Optimize console includes a simulator.
[03:15] Ben: (switching to cost model) Scenario A: hosted baseline — no caching, default batching. For 1M tokens we estimate $X — sorry, the shared sheet has the per-token line items, there's some OCR in the export so I'll paste the numbers after. Scenario B: prefix/KV cache + adaptive batching — cost drops ~35% at same latency SLO because we amortize per-token compute and reduce repeated decoding. Scenario C: dedicated pool with higher batch sizes yields ~45% cost savings but requires a commit and has less elasticity.
[04:10] Tom: On the security front, if we cache prefixes are there any PII leakage risks? we'll need to show clear TTLs and KMS controls.
[04:20] Priya: Absolutely — cache entries are encrypted at rest with customer KMS, and we can set TTLs per-prefix. For PII we recommend aggressive TTLs plus deterministic scrubbers pre-ingestion. We'll share the SOC2 + KMS playbook. Also, audit logs track cache gets/puts.
[05:00] Claire: That sounds good — are audit logs per-token? we need to tie requests back to cases for compliance.
[05:08] Priya: Audit events include request id, user id (if provided), model version, and cache hit/miss status. We don't log raw prompt text by default in compliance mode unless you opt in.
[05:32] Ben: Back to batching: Optimize suggests continuous batching with a latency budget. For your UI flows we target p95 < 400ms. With small window batching (10-20ms microbatch) you can get higher throughput but latency edges up. The console has a slider to set batching window and it simulates token tail latency.
[06:15] Raj: If we do dedicated GPUs, does the KV cache live in-GPU memory or in Redis?
[06:21] Ben: Primary KV store is in-GPU memory for fastest access; we persist cold copies in a distributed cache (can be Redis or the Redwood-managed store) for rehydration. Dedicated pools keep more KV resident because you own the workers. If you have limited GPU memory, we suggest partial prefix caching — only cache top 200 prefixes.
[06:55] Maya: Can we do hybrid routing — like critical flows to dedicated, everything else to hosted?
[06:58] Ben: Yep that's our recommended approach for many customers. Optimize lets you configure routing policies by route/label, latency SLO, or cost threshold. You can set a fallthrough to hosted if dedicated saturation > 80%.
[07:28] Alice: quick note: cost numbers below are illustrative on call but we'll update the spreadsheet. Ben, you had a small simulation you wanted to run live with their sample traffic?
[07:36] Ben: Yes, I'll run the sim for three scenarios. Loading sample trace — this might stutter a sec, the web console will throttle while it replays.
[07:52] [08:00] Ben: (simulation) Ok baseline run complete: average latency 310ms, p95 420ms, cost per 1M tokens $9.80 (hosted baseline). Now B: enable prefix KV with 50% hit — average latency 260ms, p95 370ms, cost per 1M tokens $6.40. C: dedicated w larger batches — average latency 290ms p95 360ms cost per 1M tokens $5.30 but requires commit.
[08:45] Claire: The dedicated p95 is similar to B, yet lower cost — curious about burst handling for claims surges.
[08:52] Ben: Good catch. Dedicated reduces unit cost but lacks instant elasticity. We recommend burst pools configured in Dedicated to allow short-term autoscale onto spare capacity, or route bursts to hosted as overflow. That still keeps most traffic on dedicated.
[09:20] Raj: For the hits, are you counting prefix collisions across users — e.g., similar language across different claim descriptions?
[09:30] Ben: The hit model considers exact prefix matches as well as normalized prompts — we provide canonicalization rules so semantically similar but not token-identical prompts can sometimes map to same cached key if you configure the preprocessor. There are tradeoffs: more aggressive canonicalization increases hit rate but may reduce the fidelity of responses for nuanced prompts.
[10:05] Maya: Any visibility for us into what prefixes are being cached? we want to budget and also see coverage for top use cases.
[10:12] Ben: Yes, Optimize exposes a prefix heatmap — shows top prefixes, hit rates, and memory footprint. You can download the top-k coverage CSV.
[10:30] [11:00] Priya: On encryption/key mgmt, Argus wants BYOK — bring-your-own-key. We support KMS integrations with major cloud KMS and HSM-like offerings. For private/on-prem deployments we offer customer-controlled HSM options.
[11:45] Tom: Great; do you have attestation docs for on-prem?
[11:48] Priya: We'll attach the deployment checklist and the attestation snippets. I'll follow up with concrete docs.
[12:05] Ben: (demoing console: heatmap) Here's the heatmap. You can see top 50 prefixes cover ~38% of requests in your trace. That aligns with the 40-60% hit assumption earlier. If Argus focuses on templating responses and canonicalization, you can push coverage higher quickly.
[12:48] Claire: Is there a recommended TTL for claims-related prefixes? some are sensitive for a few hours only.
[12:55] Ben: TTL depends on sensitivity. For PII we recommend under 6 hours, for non-PII UI templates you can go days. We also recommend a recency-weighted eviction that keeps frequently hit prefixes longer.
[13:20] Raj: About billing — does Redwood bill cache hits separately? or it's all baked into token billing?
[13:27] Alice: Cache hit behavior reduces billed tokens because fewer compute tokens are produced; however there are small storage and EH (engineering headroom) charges for persistent KV storage in Dedicated. We'll show line items in the cost model.
[14:00] Ben: Let's talk about quantization + caching. If you deploy a quantized variant we can still use KV caching — sometimes quantization slightly changes the KV layout and you need a consistent model version across warm workers. So rolling upgrades must consider cache invalidation. Optimize has a model-version aware cache scoping to avoid stale KV collisions.
[14:40] Maya: So if we switch model versions during a canary, do we risk wrong inference from leftover cache?
[14:47] Ben: No, we scope the cache by model-version tag. During canary, new model's KV namespace is separate. You can also do cross-version warmup by replaying prefixes to populate the new cache.
[15:10] Claire: Ok, what about functional tests — can we run an A/B where we compare baseline vs cached responses for quality drift?
[15:18] Ben: Yes, Optimize has an evaluation harness that runs prompt sets across variants and reports diffs in output distributions, hallucination rates, and token counts. That helps guard against quality regressions when increasing canonicalization or cache TTLs.
[15:42] Raj: For the 72-hour sandbox, what's the expected setup time and what telemetry will we see?
[15:49] Ben: We can stand one up in 48 hours if you provide traces and access. Telemetry includes per-route token counts, per-prefix hit/miss, p50/p95 latency, and memory footprint. We'll also give a live dashboard and exportable CSV.
[16:12] Alice: Quick tangent — competitor question: you mentioned ModelServeX earlier. Where do you see Redwood differing specifically on the caching side?
[16:18] Ben: ModelServeX has good batching, but their cache is more manual. Redwood Optimize is opinionated: automatic prefix detection, prefetch suggestions, tie-ins with routing and cost sims. It closes the loop between observed traffic and concrete batching/caching recommendations.
[16:45] Claire: Any limit on number of prefixes? we might have thousands across product lines.
[16:50] Ben: Limits are mainly memory-bound. Optimize will show memory usage and recommend a top-k caching strategy. For very large prefix sets we recommend a two-tier approach: hot in-GPU KV and warm in Redis.
[17:10] Maya: If someone crafts adversarial prompts to poison caches, how do you prevent that?
[17:18] Priya: We support validation hooks and allowlist/denylist for prefixes. You can also set per-source rate limits to reduce amplification. We'll include recommended validation rules in the onboarding playbook.
[17:40] [18:00] Ben: (running another scenario) Now I'm toggling canonicalization aggressiveness from strict to fuzzy; hit rate goes from 50% to 65% but quality diffs increase slightly in the eval harness — shows a 2% increase in odd completions for the fuzzy mode. So we typically recommend incremental canonicalization with eval monitoring.
[18:40] Claire: Good — we'll need that A/B report.
[18:44] Ben: Noted. We'll push the harness results into the sandbox dashboard.
[19:02] Raj: On the networking side, for private deployment, does the prefix cache metadata ever leave the VPC?
[19:09] Priya: No — in Private mode metadata and keys remain in customer VPC. For hosted we do not log raw prompt text unless explicitly configured; cache keys can be hashed and optionally salted with your key.
[19:32] Alice: Quick walk-through of the pricing sheet — I'm going to paste main lines in chat. Hosted token compute line, storage line for KV snapshots, dedicated amortized GPU costs, burst pool surcharge. (chat paste)
[19:58] Claire: I see a line for "cache storage" — how is that billed if we use Redwood-managed Redis?
[20:05] Alice: That's billed as a small monthly fee plus egress for snapshot restores. If you bring your own Redis in VPC, we don't charge for managed cache but there may be egress if cross-region.
[20:30] Ben: Let's cover a runbook for common incidents: cache corruption, cache warming failures, and saturation. In each case Optimize exposes diagnostics — top errors, alignment mismatches, and warmup queues. The fallback policy is to route to a safe hosted variant.
[20:58] Tom: On retention, the compliance team will want to see deletion proofs for cache entries — can you support attestations?
[21:05] Priya: Yes, we provide deletion audit events and can produce attestations for on-prem/private installs. For hosted customers we provide compliance reports in the enterprise package.
[21:32] Ben: Demo note — there's a small transcription glitch in the auto notes that says 'prefetch' as 'pre-fetch' sometimes, ignore the dash.
[21:48] Claire: (laughs) noted.
[22:00] Ben: (goes to the sandbox plan slide) For the 72-hour sandbox I propose three stages: day 0-1 mirror (replay) warmup, day 1-2 ramp traffic to 50% production cap, day 2-3 evaluate metrics and run the eval harness. We'll provide a playbook with checkpoints each 8 hours.
[22:32] Raj: For the replay, are we sampling or full fidelity? our logs are large.
[22:36] Ben: We prefer sampling at first — focus on UI flows and top 1000 prefixes. If needed, you can run a larger replay once we confirm room.
[22:58] Maya: Do you have a recommended slice for claims chat vs. policy search?
[23:03] Ben: Yes, separate routes for UI short completions (high QPS, low tokens) and longer explanatory flows (low QPS, high tokens). For short flows we prioritize low latency and prefix caching; for long flows we prefer batch-friendly quantized models.
[23:30] Claire: Will the sandbox produce estimated cost savings for a month once we scale to full production?
[23:36] Ben: Yes, the cost sim extrapolates to monthly and annual numbers. We'll include three scenarios and sensitivity bands for hit rate and batch size assumptions.
[24:00] [24:30] Priya: I'll cover security next. For SSO/SAML and RBAC, you can map to org roles. We also support fine-grained role policies almost to route level. For audit we can forward logs to your SIEM in real-time via secure connectors.
[24:58] Tom: Good. Can you show the audit event format?
[25:02] Priya: (shares sample) Each event: timestamp, request_id, route, model_version, cache_hit, user_hash (pseudonymized), action. We can remove user_hash and replace with case_id if Argus prefers.
[25:25] Raj: Do we get encrypted backups of KV snapshots?
[25:29] Priya: Yes snapshots are encrypted and we can store in your own S3 bucket if you want full control.
[25:50] Ben: (returns to console) Quick Q&A: Claire asked earlier about TTL recommendations. There's an 'auto-suggest TTL' button that analyzes prefix frequency and recommends per-prefix TTLs to meet a target memory budget.
[26:12] Claire: That seems useful. I'd like to see that in the sandbox.
[26:18] Ben: We'll enable it.
[26:30] [27:00] Alice: We're nearing the end; let's summarize next steps. Alice: Redwood to provision sandbox; Ben to run the sim and push cost spreadsheet; Priya to attach security docs; Argus to provide sample trace and SSO contact.
[27:15] Claire: Agreed. Can we have an internal review with procurement? they might need the pricing breakout.
[27:20] Alice: Yes — I'll include procurement-friendly lines in the deck.
[27:42] Raj: Small thing: network egress — if we route burst to hosted, any egress fees between VPC and Redwood?
[27:48] Priya: If you're in Private deployment, no egress within VPC. If you use hybrid where traffic leaves your VPC to Redwood hosted, standard provider egress applies. We'll map this in the spreadsheet.
[28:10] [29:00] Ben: Quick demo wrap-up — we also show a live example of cache prefetching: when a claim is opened the orchestration can proactively warm the prefix set for that user's next expected prompts. That reduces first-request latency substantially.
[29:26] Maya: How do you predict 'next expected prompts'? is it heuristic based?
[29:31] Ben: Heuristic + lightweight ML model for next-turn prediction; customers can plug in their own predictor. It's opt-in because it requires additional telemetry.
[29:55] Claire: We'll likely opt-in for predicted prefetching for priority customers.
[30:02] Ben: Ok I'll include prefetch in the sandbox.
[30:20] Alice: Anything else from Argus?
[30:24] Tom: One last security question: deletion proof latency — how quickly can we purge a cache entry and produce an audit?
[30:30] Priya: Purge is immediate; audit event is generated within seconds and we can provide a signed attestation that it occurred. For on-prem we can do a live proof.
[30:48] Claire: Great, thanks.
[31:00] Ben: (minor pause) there's a quick note in the console about model-quantization interplay, I want to show a short graph. (shares) If you quantize 4-bit, compute drops ~40% but warmup time for cache slightly increases due to mapping overhead. It still often wins for long tail cost.
[31:40] Raj: That's ok for our long explanatory tasks.
[31:45] Ben: Final checklist: security docs, sandbox traces, pricing spreadsheet. We'll follow up by EOD Monday.
[31:58] Alice: thanks all. we'll send calendar invite for security review.
[32:06] Claire: thanks, this was helpful.
[32:10] (meeting ends)

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-attribution and dropped punctuation from the auto-transcript; some product names may appear with hyphens or slightly different capitalization (Optimize vs Optmize).
